newsitem.title: IRAN: NIOC NOT TO INCREASE ASIA EXPORTS TO OVER 40 PCT.
newsitem.headline: NIOC NOT TO INCREASE ASIA EXPORTS TO OVER 40 PCT.

text.p: National Iranian Oil Co (NIOC) is not planning to lift crude exports to higher value east of Suez markets to more than 40 percent of its total sales, Vice Petroleum Minister Ghanimi Fard said on Thursday.

Fard said that despite the higher price Iranian crudes could fetch in Asia compared to west of Suez, NIOC would continue its current "40-40-20" sales strategy rather than run the risk of future potential marketing problems.
Almost 40 percent of Iran's 2.5 million barrels per day (bpd) crude exports go east of Suez, 40 percent to Europe and the remaining 20 percent to Africa and the Americas, Fard said.
"We are not trying to increase the volume more than 40 percent to the east," he told Reuters in an interview at the petroleum ministry in Tehran.
"We should penetrate the crude in all markets so no kind of possible problem in the future can hurt the marketing of the crude of Iran."
Fard, who also heads NIOC's marketing department, agreed with a description of the 40-40-20 policy as a "safety-net against possible sanctions."
NIOC lost all its U.S. crude customers -- which were NIOC's main buyers -- in 1995 when President Bill Clinton stopped the $4 billion trade between NIOC and U.S. oil firms.

Industry analysts have expected NIOC to increase its sales east of Suez where mainly Japanese and South Korean refiners pay higher prices than their European counterparts because of NIOC's different formula pricing.

NIOC earlier this year tied up a major supply crude supply deal with China, prompting industry speculation that NIOC would increasingly sell its 2.5 million bpd or exports to Asian market at the expense of European firms.
In 1970 Iran sold 62.6 percent of its crude to Asia.
Italy, Britain, France and Belgium headed NIOC's European client list, while Canada, Central American and South American firms also regularly bought Iranian crude, he said.
Fard said Asian customers accounted for more incremental sales above base term contract volumes but that this did not represent a significant marketing switch.
"The 40 percent (sales to Asia) is the target that we have in order to keep it balanced," he said.
"Frankly speaking there has not been any attempt on NIOC's side to decrease the exports to good and long-term clients -- including traders -- that we have in the West."
Iran's crude exports bring in an annual $18 billion or 40 percent of total government revenue.
